name: Beth Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential and your name won't be attached. What does a usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the motor-claims enquiries row for an insurer. Someone calls after a crash because the hire car was not booked or the repairer says the insurer has not approved a part, and I follow the file until the story matches. I have a two-year college diploma in business administration and am one of the stronger people on unusual cases, but I have never used the AI assistant.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you rely on, and who is at home with you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rely on dated repair notes and a little index of garage phone numbers, not a summary someone else produced. My husband Owen works fixed hours at a museum front desk, and our grown daughter rents with friends. Our pay is ordinary rather than generous, and we have about five months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the claims row that the paperwork still has to agree with the garage before we promise a hire car. A small shortcut might save typing, but a wrong approval takes longer to undo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my work to continue because people still ring when a repairer and insurer disagree. Owen's museum hours are steady and five months saved covers ordinary trouble, so I can sleep in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep checking repair dates against the garage notes and teach the newer agents how to spot an approval entered on the wrong claim. In the first year of AI Plateau I would ask our supervisor to keep a written rule that the original repair record wins if a summary conflicts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with the usual irritation at a muddled file. I do not feel pushed to take a course just to use a shortcut I distrust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What detail caught that wrong part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A garage once rang me with a part ordered for the wrong car because two surnames matched. The vehicle number, not the neat description, told us which claim was real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend from the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we would leave our five months saved alone. A working kitchen floor does not need replacing because a computer saved my team a few minutes.

I would say the **vehicle number** beats a neat but wrong summary.
think: I expect my **claims work** to continue under small change.
I trust our **five-month reserve** and Owen's steady museum hours for ordinary trouble.
do: Keep checking **repair dates** and teach new agents to catch wrong-claim approvals.
Ask for a **written original-record rule** when an AI summary conflicts.
feel: I feel **calm** about wages and wary of muddled summaries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say routine bookings and claim checks could move to software, leaving us fewer but nastier calls. I would ask for the paid hours assigned to those calls before anyone says my lead job is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My difficult-case skill may still matter, but a smaller row means fewer paid seats. I could lose a day a week even if my title stays on the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep a log of cases where a repairer calls back after an automated approval and ask the supervisor for the proposed paid complex-claims rota. If my own shifts fall in the first year routine cases move, I would compare posted local insurance desks by written full-week wages and hours, and leave only after a signed offer covers our bills and the bus fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a shorter paid week, though I can still check the files and the adverts. A title on the door does not tell my husband Owen and me what arrives on payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you count a return call?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count each return call against the first approval, not as a new success. The garage cannot fit a part because a dashboard says the case closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you work at another insurer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not assume the nearby insurer is hiring simply because its sign is lit. I would look at a posted paid vacancy, then its actual rota and travel cost, before giving up this paid seat.

say: I would ask for **paid complex-claim hours** before calling my lead role safe.
I would say **return calls** belong in the same claim's record.
think: I could lose **paid shifts** when routine cases move.
I cannot count on **nearby vacancies** without an actual posting.
do: Log **repeat garage calls** and request the planned paid complex-claims rota.
After **my shifts fall**, compare posted insurance work; leave only with signed weekly wages and hours covering bills after bus fare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a shorter paid week despite my skill.

fieldNote: Her **lead title** may remain while the paid rota shrinks.
A move depends on a **posted vacancy** and signed bill-covering full-week terms after travel, while she retains current paid calls.

steps.text: Keep a log of repeat garage calls and ask for the paid complex-claims rota

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Owen that thinking AI by 2028 can sort claims and bookings before we get a turn at the file. Hands-on repair robots arrive around 2031, but my phone work faces the earlier date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the insurer could end most of my paid desk hours quickly. Five months saved and Owen's museum wage buy a search period, not a long life without my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would collect the last six payslips and make a list of rent, food and travel with Owen, then ask my manager when paid human appeals would end. If most desk hours end in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid visitor-service work at the local museum where Owen works; I would accept only written weekly wages and hours covering our bills after bus fare, and keep any paid claims shifts still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the size and speed of the possible loss, but not without a phone or a notebook. Five months saved is enough to search carefully, not enough to stay idle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a museum vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the museum's visitor desk has a real paid vacancy rather than a volunteer rota. Owen's job there does not guarantee that I can walk into another one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter pay for a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter can hear us out, but she has her own rent. We would not put her wages into our budget unless she offered help and could spare it.

I would ask when **paid human appeals** would end.
think: I expect **most desk hours** could end quickly.
I cannot replace my **own wage** for long with five months saved and Owen's pay.
do: Collect **six payslips** and list household bills while asking about the paid appeal end date.

feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely large hours cut, though I can search.
S2.quote: Five months saved is enough to search carefully, not enough to stay idle.
fieldNote: She does not treat **Owen's museum role** as a guaranteed opening.
She keeps **available paid claims shifts** during the search without assuming Owen can supply a museum vacancy.

steps.text: Keep paid claims shifts while asking manager when human appeal hours would end

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the claims row a few years lets us see how many genuine dispute cases are left, if the employer shares the paid hours. Thinking AI could take file decisions by 2031; repair robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still do hard claims, but the insurer might not pay a full week of leads. At 63 I cannot say what income would replace my wage if I wanted fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask our supervisor for a monthly figure on paid dispute hours and put it beside our return-call log. I would keep my paid claims shifts; if they fall in the first year after 2031, I would ask at the local repairers' office whether it has posted paid customer-desk work, checking written wages and hours and the bus timetable before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the paid week, not curious about another computer lesson. I can ask a repairer what its desk really does before treating it as a fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the repairers office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the desk approves a repair or just tells a driver where to park. Those are different jobs, and I am qualified for one only if someone shows me the actual work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not call 63 a stopping point. Owen and I would need written income figures and actual bills before deciding whether a shorter week is affordable.

I would explain **2031 file AI** arrives before 2034 repair robots.
think: I might keep **hard claims** while losing a full paid week.
I cannot name **replacement income** at 63 without written figures.
do: Compare **monthly dispute hours** with the return-call log while keeping paid shifts.
If shifts fall after 2031, ask about **posted repair-office work** and check written wages, hours and bus times before applying.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible loss of paid hours.
S3.quote: I can ask a repairer what its desk really does before treating it as a fallback.
fieldNote: She wants to know **actual desk duties** before treating repair-office work as a fallback.
A conditional enquiry follows **her own hours falling**, with written wages and bus times checked.

steps.text: Compare monthly paid dispute hours with repeat garage calls while keeping paid claims shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to record which claims still need a person, without pretending that record guarantees us a wage. Thinking AI reaches claims by 2036 and capable repair robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might prefer fewer hours, but I do not know the income that would replace the claims wage. Five months saved is a buffer, not a reason to choose a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen and I would get actual income statements and compare them with a full year of bills this winter. I would keep the paid dispute row and ask annually for its written hours; after 2036 I would reduce work only if verified income covered our bills, otherwise keep the paid shifts actually offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later claims work, but steady about today's wages. I can check one year's figures at a time without inventing a pension amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which costs belong beside wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count our rent and travel in the same column as the wages, not assume they get cheaper with age. If the dispute row shrinks, the written rota will show us first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter help later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter has her own plans and rent. I will not turn her visits into a line of income because she has not offered that.

say: I would use the **decade** to record paid human claim work.
I would say **2036 claims AI** comes before 2039 repair robots.
think: I cannot name **income replacing wages** at 68.
I see **five months saved** as a buffer rather than retirement pay.
do: Compare **income statements** with a full year of bills alongside Owen.
Keep **paid disputes** and ask yearly for written hours; reduce work only if verified income covers bills.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later work while current wages are steady.
S4.quote: Five months saved is a buffer, not a reason to choose a retirement date.
fieldNote: She checks **actual income** before reducing paid work and assumes no pension right.
She continues **available paid claims** if verified income does not cover bills.

steps.text: Keep paid claims disputes and ask each year for the written human dispute rota

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because a five-month reserve disappears faster than a stable job can be found. Written paid appeals, a real vacancy and time to inspect its duties would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the repairer's file when the software says 'approved' but the garage has no part. Somebody still has to answer that call.

headlineQuote: The garage cannot fit a part because a dashboard says the case closed.
portrait: A **58-year-old** senior motor-claims agent with a two-year business diploma and strong unusual-case skill.
She **never uses AI**, relying on repair notes, vehicle numbers and garage calls.
Owen's **steady museum wage** and five months saved help, while her own claims hours remain at risk.
She checks **real duties** and written terms before treating another desk as a fallback.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could end most desk hours before a stable paid job appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written appeal hours**, a posted paid vacancy and time to inspect its duties would help.
